title: Technical deep dive: Guardrails & performance (moderation placement)
summary: Deep dive on how to place safety filters and moderation in the inference pipeline without violating latency SLOs. Discussed inline vs async moderation, lightweight pre-filters, batching/KV cache effects, quantization impact on safety model performance, and VPC/on-prem deployment tradeoffs. Agreed to run 95th-percentile latency microbenchmarks with moderation enabled and test async fallback flows.
topics: safety filter overhead and latency impact
quantization and model fidelity for safety classifiers
action_items: Alex Morgan: Share moderation cost + latency spreadsheet and example configs by 2025-05-20
Priya Shah: Run end-to-end microbench with moderation inline and async for their workload (50/95/99 pct) and upload results by 2025-05-22
Miguel Alvarez (customer): Provide sample prompt distribution and PII-sensitive endpoints by 2025-05-18
Daniel Wu: Provide recommended kernel/quantization profile for their A100 and T4 nodes by 2025-05-23
next_steps: Run bench with inline moderation on Dedicated and Private setup
Test async moderation path that returns provisional response and updates if blocked
Share security docs and SOC2 audit excerpt
Schedule follow-up sync after microbench results (tentatively 2025-05-27)
transcript:
[00:00] Alex Morgan: Hey everyone, thanks for joining. we'll kick off the deep dive on guardrails and performance, specifically moderation placement and the overhead. can you all hear me?
[00:05] John Miller: yes, loud and clear. we wanted to understand best practices — we have tight 95th percentile latency SLOs for customer-facing chat and also strict PHI rules.
[00:12] Priya Shah (SE): quick agenda — 1) where to run safety checks (inline v async), 2) cost and latency tradeoffs, 3) how KV cache and batching change the math, 4) quantization concerns for safety models, 5) deployment constraints (VPC/on-prem).
[00:25] Sarah Lee (Customer): brief context — prod traffic spikes to ~120 rps, avg token length 80, tail goes up with long sessions. currently using an internal LLM with a homegrown classifier; it's adding ~120-200ms per request and spikes mess up our p95.
[00:40] Alex Morgan: thanks. two high-level patterns we recommend: inline moderation (call safety classifier in the same request path before returning final content) and async/post-hoc moderation (return provisional content, then block/recall or patch if violation detected).
[00:55] Miguel Alvarez: our compliance team prefers blocking before response, but product is worried about latency. is there a middle ground?
[01:02] Priya Shah: yes — we often use a lightweight pre-filter (regex + small token-level heuristic model) inline, then run a stronger safety classifier async or on a cached copy. the pre-filter catches majority of low-hanging PII and obvious violations with <10ms overhead. heavier model runs can be batched or run on GPUs with KV cache to speed up.
[01:20] Sarah Lee: how does batching interact? our bursty traffic means batching sometimes helps, but we also have low-latency single-user flows.
[01:30] Daniel Wu: batching helps amortize moderation cost if you can tolerate a few extra ms. for GPU-backed safety models we see throughput gains, but real effect depends on sequence length and how many concurrent requests land in the batch. also, batching can hurt p95 for single-shot flows unless you set a max wait time.
[01:45] Priya Shah: important nuance — KV cache is only helpful for the main generation model; safety classifier usually runs on the full output or on a compact representation. if you run safety inline before final generate you'll miss cached-only tokens; we sometimes run the classifier on a compact prefix or a summary to keep latency low.
[02:05] Alex Morgan: a pattern we've used at customers: 1) pre-filter inline (fast), 2) generate with KV cache and async logging, 3) run stronger safety classifier async on final output and if flagged, route follow-up mitigation (suppress, redact, human review). that gives best user experience while meeting compliance for many cases.
[02:25] John Miller: but for PHI we need deterministic blocking before return. can Redwood support that with Dedicated or Private?
[02:31] Priya Shah: yes — Dedicated or Private allows you to colocate safety models in the same VPC/on-prem environment so cross-network latency is predictable. for strict blocking you run both the generator and classifier inline on Dedicated hosts; cost will be higher but p95 can be kept low with proper autoscaling and batching policies.
[02:47] Sarah Lee: any numbers on overhead? rough numbers are fine.
[02:51] Priya Shah: rough empirical: a small on-CPU heuristic filter ~5-15ms, a medium safety classifier on GPU (FP16) ~40-120ms depending on sequence length and quantization, a large safety model (e.g., stricter classifier) could add 150-400ms. quantization to int8 can reduce times ~20-40% but sometimes hurts classifier recall — must validate on your eval set.
[03:15] Miguel Alvarez: that variance is concerning. is there guidance on where to place filters to hit p95 targets?
[03:20] Priya Shah: if p95 target is tight (<200ms), we recommend pre-filter inline + move heavy classifier async or behind a fast failover. if p95 can be looser, colocate both inline on Dedicated with autoscale and prefer quantized classifiers with tuned kernels. also set graceful degradation: fallback to cached or shorter responses when moderation path is saturated.
[03:39] Alex Morgan: note about kernel selection — our runtime picks optimized kernels based on model shape. for quantized safety models we prefer per-channel quantization and fused kernels, which reduce overhead. Daniel, any infra comments?
[03:50] Daniel Wu: yes — on A100 we saw kernel-level gains at long sequence lengths; on T4 smaller models with int8 gave best perf. for Private deployments, ensure inter-node NVLink or local GPUs for minimal cross-host latency. also watch for CPU-side overhead in pre/post-processing (tokenization, detoken).
[04:10] Sarah Lee: will quantization hurt safety recall? we need to be careful not to increase false negatives.
[04:14] Priya Shah: totally. quantization can change logits and marginal decisions. we always recommend running your safety evals (we can help) with the quantized model in the loop. sometimes a hybrid approach works: quantize generator but keep safety classifier in fp16 or slightly higher precision.
[04:31] John Miller: what about placement in the network for VPC/on-prem? e.g., if we host generator in a private subnet and safety classifier in a different subnet, network hops matter, right?
[04:40] Daniel Wu: yes. each cross-subnet hop adds RTT and jitter. best to colocate generator + classifier on same subnet or host for inline blocking. if governance requires separate accounts, use high-throughput private peering and make sure MTU and routing are optimized.
[04:55] Priya Shah: another option is to run a small local safety model inline for blocking, and mirror full outputs to a heavier classifier in another region for audit and post-hoc checks. that satisfies auditing while protecting latency.
[05:08] Miguel Alvarez: how do we handle moderation failures? we need audit logs and an abuse review pipeline.
[05:12] Alex Morgan: Redwood Console supports token-level traces and audit logs. for Private, logs can be forwarded to your SIEM or retained on-prem. for failures we recommend a queue-driven human review flow and automated ML retraining when false positives/negatives exceed thresholds.
[05:30] Sarah Lee: any suggestions on experiments to run?
[05:33] Priya Shah: run three bench variants: 1) baseline (no moderation), 2) inline lightweight pre-filter + async heavy classifier, 3) full inline heavy classifier. measure p50/p95/p99 latency, token throughput, cost per 1M tokens, and safety recall/precision on your dev prompts.
[05:50] Alex Morgan: we'll provide a spreadsheet with cost and latency models; Priya will run the microbench on a snapshot of your prompt set. Daniel will produce recommended quant/profile for their hardware.
[06:03] John Miller: what about canarying changes in production? we need stepwise rollouts for safety rule updates.
[06:09] Rita Gomez (PM): Redwood supports canary rollouts and traffic splits by model version; you can route a small % of prod traffic to a new safety classifier and monitor regressions. we also have automatic rollback on metric regressions.
[06:22] Sarah Lee: any gotchas when combining batching with safety?
[06:25] Priya Shah: yes — batching tends to hide single-request latency; ensure per-request deadlines and max batch wait times are configured. also be careful with stateful sessions — KV cache interactions may mean safety checks need to inspect full session context. if you truncate context to speed up, you may miss earlier offending content.
[06:45] Alex Morgan: quick note on async mitigation UX — when a later check blocks content, options are: suppress response, redact offending spans and resend, show a warning + escalate to human, or present a provisional message ("we're reviewing this"). choose based on regulatory need.
[07:00] Miguel Alvarez: good, that'll help. can you send over SOC2 snippets and a sample architecture showing inline + async paths?
[07:05] Alex Morgan: yes, we'll share SOC2 excerpts and a short architecture diagram. link to benchmark spreadsheet placeholder: https://redwood.example.com/benchmarks/novahealth-moderation-v1 (will send final).
[07:18] John Miller: thanks. one last question — is there an easy way to run safety classifiers as serverless functions within Redwood Private?
[07:25] Daniel Wu: we support containerized safety services in Private; you can register them as model endpoints or sidecars. serverless-style cold starts might hurt latency so warm-up policies are recommended.
[07:35] Sarah Lee: ok thanks, this was helpful.
[07:38] Alex Morgan: recap: Redwood to share cost/latency spreadsheet, Priya to run microbench and upload results, Daniel to give kernel/quant profiles, customer to share prompt set and security contacts. schedule follow-up next week. thanks all.
[07:50] (meeting ends)
